summary: Defines MIB objects for managing remote network monitoring devices, often called probes, with SNMP. It is a draft standard. It has been replaced by RFC 2819.

plainLanguage.summary: Little watchers placed around a network that record what passes by, and gauges to read what they saw.

subtitle: Management information base for remote network monitoring devices.

tldr.problem: Networks need monitoring devices that can collect statistics, detect problems, and work offline when management stations are unavailable. These remote probes need a standard way to be queried and configured.
tldr.mechanism: RMON defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with groups of objects that probes can implement: statistics collection, history, alarms, host tracking, traffic matrix analysis, packet capture, and event notification.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can deploy multiple monitoring probes across different segments and control them via SNMP, allowing both local analysis and remote management. RFC 2819 replaced this version with extensions.

sections.title: What RMON Is
sections.content:
Remote Network Monitoring (RMON) devices are standalone probes that monitor network segments and report what they see back to management stations. This MIB defines the objects that describe and control these probes using SNMP, the Simple Network Management Protocol.

Unlike earlier approaches where a manager polls individual network devices, RMON probes are dedicated appliances that sit on the network and continuously gather statistics, detect problems, and store data. Even when the management station is offline, the probe keeps working and can alert operators when something goes wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: An RMON probe is like a security camera on your network: it watches continuously and records what happens, even when nobody is looking.

sections.title: Remote Monitoring Goals
sections.content: RMON was designed with several key objectives. Offline operation: probes work independently and can notify management stations when exceptional conditions occur, reducing bandwidth on WAN links. Proactive monitoring: probes run diagnostics continuously and log performance data, making them available at the moment a failure happens. Problem detection: the probe recognizes configured error conditions and events, logging them and sending notifications. Value-added data: because probes sit directly on the monitored segment, they can identify the hosts generating the most traffic or errors. Multiple managers: several management stations can share the same probe's resources.
sections.plainLanguage: RMON probes are always watching, remember what they see, spot problems automatically, and tell a human operator when something is wrong.

sections.title: MIB Groups and Structure
sections.content:
The RMON MIB organizes its objects into functional groups. The Ethernet Statistics Group tracks errors, collisions, and packet counts on each monitored interface. The History Group records periodic samples for later analysis. The Alarm Group monitors variables against thresholds and triggers events. The Host Group discovers and tracks devices on the network by learning their MAC addresses. The HostTopN Group produces ranked reports of top talkers. The Matrix Group records traffic between pairs of addresses. The Filter Group matches packets against patterns, and the Packet Capture Group stores matched packets for inspection. The Event Group controls notifications.

All groups are optional except system and interfaces. If a probe implements a group, it must implement all objects in that group.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is like a filing cabinet with different drawers: statistics, history, alarms, devices, top talkers, conversations, filters, captured packets, and events.

sections.title: Control and Resource Sharing
sections.content:
RMON devices manage resources shared among multiple management stations. Each function has an owner field that identifies who configured it—either a specific management station, the probe itself (marked as 'monitor'), or another operator. This allows management stations to find resources they own, and administrators to manage disputes over limited resources like memory and processing power.

Configuration works through control tables (read-write) that describe what to do and data tables (read-only) that hold results. To change configuration, a manager marks the control entry invalid, deleting it and any associated data, then creates a new entry with updated parameters. This approach prevents parameter changes from breaking running operations and helps reclaim resources when they are no longer needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the probe like a shared kitchen: you write your name on the timer before you use the oven, and when you are done, you clean up so someone else can use it.

sections.title: Status and Adoption
sections.content: RFC 1757 is a Draft Standard and is now Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 2819, which added extensions for additional media types like Token Ring and FDDI, and refined the model. The fundamental concepts in 1757 remain influential in modern network monitoring, though SNMP-based monitoring has evolved with new protocols and approaches for large-scale deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: This design was very successful and became the foundation for more advanced network monitoring, though the specific details have been updated over time.
